job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Victor Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior analyst on the equities team at Lomond Capital, a mid-size asset manager in Edinburgh. I started in September. I'm up at six, in by seven for the morning call, then I build screens of companies and write short notes for the portfolio managers. I share a flat in Leith with a lad from uni who's doing law, and we both live in the gym.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and what's the worst?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is when one of my notes actually changes a decision, which has happened twice. The worst is the hours before earnings, when I'm eating a sandwich at my desk at ten at night. I use AI constantly, to summarise filings and to draft the first version of a note. My parents, a surveyor and a school secretary, said they'd help if anything went wrong, so I can take a few risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful and overhyped, and I'd leave it at that. At work I'd say the tools save time, but the real value is still in judging what matters. I'd probably post a joke about the hype to my uni group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my edge, since I'm good with the tools and also good at the actual work. Lomond is growing and Edinburgh has a lot of finance, so I'm not worried. I'd still be a junior for a few years, but that's normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the CFA exams, one level a year, and keep building screens. I'd try to get a seat at the stock-picking meetings, and I'd save about 35 percent of my pay. I'd also put £200 a month into my own small portfolio, because I should practise what I research.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like it when the world is predictable enough to plan in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI all day. How much of your edge would vanish if it stopped improving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, yes. The tools help me read twenty pages in two minutes, but the thinking about whether management is lying to you is still mine. I'd lose some speed, but the stuff that makes me worth keeping isn't speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your own pressures be, even then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Competition, honestly. There are always four other graduates after the same promotion. And markets can turn, a bad year and a team cuts juniors, nothing to do with AI. I'd be fine, but I'd be watching my results.

say: I'd say the tools save time, but the real value is **judging what matters**.
I'd post a **joke** about the hype in my uni group chat.
think: I keep my **edge**, since I'm good with the tools and the actual work.
Lomond is growing and Edinburgh has lots of **finance**, so I'm not worried.
do: Keep going with the **CFA** exams, one level a year.
Get a seat at the **stock-picking** meetings.
Save **35 percent** of pay and put £200 a month into my own portfolio.
feel: I feel **calm**, because I like a world I can plan in.
S0.quote: The thinking about whether management is lying to you is still mine.
fieldNote: Victor is **confident**, with a cushion, plenty of local jobs and strong tool skills.
His worry is **competition** and the market cycle, not AI.
He treats judgement as his **edge**, a theme throughout.

steps.text: Pass CFA Level One next year
Use AI to read filings faster, then check by hand
Save 35 percent of my pay each month
Put £200 a month into my own stock portfolio

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving fast, and everyone in finance should accept that. I'd say to the portfolio managers that we could use the tools more, and I'd offer to build a prototype. I wouldn't complain, because that doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the first-year analyst job is probably on the way out. Summaries, screens and first drafts, which is most of what I do, are the thinking tasks on the list. Lomond will hire fewer of us and expect more from each. I'm good with the tools, but so will every other new graduate be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a tool for our team that does the screens in minutes, and I'd make sure everyone knows I built it. I'd move toward the part of the work where people talk to companies and clients, because that still needs a person. And I'd keep saving, £800 a month, so I have a cushion if the market turns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fired up. I like a challenge, but I'd be lying if I said it didn't scare me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a junior analyst's day are on the card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Summaries of filings, screens of companies, first drafts of notes and the data cleaning. I do all of those every day. What's left is the judgement and the conversations, which I'm still learning, so I'd need to learn them faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you try to stand out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person who's both good at the tools and good with the people. There are few who are both. That's my plan, and it might not work, but it's the best one I've got.

say: I'd say we should use the tools **more**, and I'd offer to build a prototype.
I wouldn't **complain**, because it doesn't help anyone.
think: Privately, the first-year **analyst** job is probably on the way out.
**Summaries**, screens and first drafts are most of what I do.
do: Build a **tool** that does the team's screens in minutes.
Move toward **client and company** conversations, which need a person.
Save **£800** a month as a cushion.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but fired up, because I like a challenge.
S1.quote: I'd become the person who's both good at the tools and good with the people.
fieldNote: Victor sees his own role in the **list**, and accepts it.
His plan is to be **both** tool-skilled and people-skilled.
He is **fired up** and ready to lead the change.

steps.text: Build a screening tool for the equities team
Learn to run company meetings and client calls
Save £800 a month as a cushion
Test new AI research tools every Friday afternoon

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and markets, firms and governments need a plan. I'd probably say I'd rather it be slowed down, but I don't think it will be. I'd say it to the portfolio managers carefully, because they might say it's overblown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my career is gone in two years. Analysing companies is thinking work, and AGI does it better and cheaper. The only people who survive are the ones who own capital or run things, and I'm neither. The robots come in three years, but they won't affect my desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save £1,200 a month and keep my spending tight. I'd move more of my own money into the assets that hold their value, like the stuff I research, but not stupidly. And I'd talk to my parents about a safety net, because I might need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's a heavy feeling, like a deadline I can't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What happens to the plan you just described?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My plan stops making sense, since the plan was to be good at the work. If AGI is the work, the plan is to get ownership or a role where a person has to be there. I'd try to move into the client side or start a small advisory outfit, anything where I'm the face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you act on the money side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my subscriptions and my gym membership and stop trying to buy stuff. I'd set up a standing order into a cash fund. And I'd tell myself I'm still ahead of most people, which is sort of true, but it wouldn't feel like enough.

say: I'd say the pace is **too fast** and markets, firms and governments need a plan.
I'd tell the managers **carefully**, since they might say it's overblown.
think: Privately, **my career is gone** in two years, since analysing companies is thinking work.
The survivors own **capital** or run things, and I'm neither.
do: Save **£1,200** a month and keep spending tight.
Move more of my own money into assets that **hold value**.
Talk to my parents about a **safety net**.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, like a deadline I can't move.
S2.quote: The only people who survive are the ones who own capital or run things, and I'm neither.
fieldNote: Victor **expects** to lose his career, and says so plainly.
He sees **ownership** as the only protection, a finance-brained answer.
His strong **cushion** doesn't calm him, because the career is what he loses.

steps.text: Save £1,200 a month in a cash fund
Cancel my gym and subscriptions
Move my own money into assets that hold value
Talk to my parents about a safety net

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a window, so let's use it. I'd say firms should retrain the people they have rather than lay them off, and governments should tax the firms that gain most. I'd say it directly, because I like to get to the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have about five years of career and then a big gap. I'd be twenty-seven, with a decent track record, and it might be enough to get into portfolio management before the window closes. If not, I'd have capital and skills to try something else. So I'm anxious but not desperate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for promotion fast, since five years is enough to get to a senior seat. I'd save £1,000 a month and invest a lot of it. I'd also learn the technical side of AI properly, maybe a night course, so I can work with the people who build it. And I'd talk to a mentor at Lomond about the long-term picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more like a race than a threat. I like races if I've got a decent start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do that two wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The winners are the people who own capital, the people who build the tools and the people who sit in the room with clients. The losers are the large middle of junior and mid-level desk workers. I'm trying to jump out of that middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think wins and who loses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me plan to win, not just survive. In two years I'm defending. In five I can move up before the shape of the job changes, and that's a big difference.

say: I'd say firms should **retrain** the people they have rather than lay them off.
I'd say governments should **tax** the firms that gain most.
think: I'd have about five years of career, then a **big gap**.
I might reach **portfolio management** before the window closes.
do: Push for a **promotion** to a senior seat within five years.
Save **£1,000** a month and invest a lot of it.
Take a night course on the **technical side** of AI.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but it's more like a race than a threat.
S3.quote: Five years lets me plan to win, not just survive.
fieldNote: Victor treats time as a **race** he can win.
He names the **middle** of desk workers as the likely losers.
His plan includes capital, **skills** and a mentor.

steps.text: Push for a promotion to a senior analyst seat
Take a night course on how AI systems are built
Save £1,000 a month and invest most of it
Ask a Lomond mentor about the long-term picture

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a lot of time, so let's do it properly. I'd say schools and firms should start now. At work I'd just say it's an interesting problem and I'd rather be inside it than outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's fine for me. By 2036 I'd be thirty-two, with ten years of experience, maybe running a team, maybe with my own firm. The change would still hit, but I'd have the time to climb up, own something and switch if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep rising at Lomond and aim to be a portfolio manager in six or seven years. I'd save for a flat and a pension from now. I'd keep using AI every day, and I'd try to build something of my own on the side, maybe an advisory tool for small investors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited. This is the one I can plan for, so I'm happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What would you aim for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to run money or run a firm. I'd have a flat in Edinburgh and be investing hard. And I'd probably help younger analysts with the tools, because it's how I got my first break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in having so long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The risk is complacency. When it's ten years away, people stop acting. I've seen it in my own savings, where I told myself I'd start later. So I'd set up automatic things now, like standing orders, so I can't forget.

say: I'd say a decade is a lot of time, so let's do it **properly**.
I'd say I'd rather be **inside** the problem than outside it.
think: I think it's **fine** for me, and by 2036 I'd be thirty-two with ten years of experience.
With ten years I'd have time to **own** something and switch if needed.
do: Aim to be a **portfolio manager** in six or seven years.
Save for a flat and a **pension** from now.
Build a small **advisory tool** for retail investors on the side.
feel: I feel **calm** and a bit excited, because this one I can plan for.
S4.quote: When it's ten years away, people stop acting.
fieldNote: Victor is **calm** because ten years fits his plan.
He names **complacency** as the risk, a self-aware point.
He wants to **own** something, which is his consistent theme.

steps.text: Aim to become a portfolio manager in six or seven years
Set up a standing order for my pension and flat savings
Build an advisory tool for small investors on the side
Buy a flat in Edinburgh by around thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my plan depends on time and two years takes it away. What would help is a government that shares the gains, a way for ordinary people to own a piece of the AI economy, and honest talk from firms about what they plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm aware I'm in a good position and still anxious, which says something. If I'm a bit scared, someone with debt and no family help must be terrified. That's the bit that worries me about how this goes.

headlineQuote: If I'm a bit scared, someone with debt and no family help must be terrified.
portrait: Victor, 22, is a **junior equities analyst** at an Edinburgh asset manager, and uses AI every day.
His parents, a surveyor and a school secretary, can help, which lets him take **risks**.
He sees summaries, screens and first drafts as his own exposed tasks, and aims for **tools and people skills**.
Calm with ten years, but **alarmed** at two, because his plan needs time he wouldn't have.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because his plan depends on time and two years takes it away.
whatWouldHelp: A government that **shares the gains**, and a way for ordinary people to own part of the AI economy.
**Honest talk** from firms about what they plan.
